module_title: Subordinate Courts and Tribunals - Basic Understanding
introduction: In India's integrated judicial system, the courts at the district level and below are called 'Subordinate Courts' because they function under the administrative control of the state's High Court. They are covered in Part VI of the Constitution (Articles 233 to 237).

core_concepts.title: District Court
core_concepts.description: It is the highest judicial body in a district. The same court has two names depending on the case it hears: When hearing civil cases (property, marriage), it is called the 'District Court'. When hearing criminal cases (theft, murder), it is called the 'Sessions Court'.

core_concepts.title: Tribunals (Basic Idea)
core_concepts.description: Tribunals are quasi-judicial bodies created to resolve specific types of disputes quickly and efficiently (like taxes, armed forces, or environment). They were not part of the original Constitution but were added later.

core_concepts.title: Lok Adalat
core_concepts.description: Known as the 'People's Court', it is an alternative dispute resolution mechanism where cases are settled through compromise and mutual consent. Its main goal is to provide fast and free justice.

important_entities.name: The Governor
important_entities.significance: The Governor of the state, in consultation with the High Court, appoints, posts, and promotes the District Judges.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: At the lower levels of the district judiciary, the officer heading civil cases is called a 'Judge' (e.g., Civil Judge), while the officer heading criminal cases is called a 'Magistrate' (e.g., Chief Judicial Magistrate).

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Visualizing the hierarchy is crucial. District and Subordinate courts form the broad base of the Indian judicial pyramid.

exam_strategy_tips: Always remember the dual role: District Judge = Civil Cases; Sessions Judge = Criminal Cases. This is a very common basic MCQ.
Decisions made by a Lok Adalat are final and binding on all parties; no appeal lies against them in any court.
